content: Pressure ulcers, also known as bedsores, are a significant health issue, affecting between 5% and 32% of patients admitted to UK District General Hospitals, depending on the patient population, and 4% to 7% of individuals in community settings. These ulcers impose a substantial burden on patients, leading to reduced quality of life and increased strain on caregivers. Additionally, they are costly for healthcare systems to manage. Treatment strategies for pressure ulcers typically include the use of wound dressings, measures to relieve pressure on the affected area, management of underlying conditions that may impede healing, and physical therapies such as electrical stimulation, laser therapy, and ultrasound. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of therapeutic ultrasound in promoting the healing of pressure ulcers. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, and Ovid CINAHL, covering literature up to April 2008. The study focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared therapeutic ultrasound with either sham ultrasound or standard treatment. Two independent reviewers screened the search results to identify relevant RCTs. Data from eligible studies were extracted using a standardized data extraction form, and efforts were made to contact study authors to obtain any missing information. A second reviewer verified the extracted data for accuracy. When the interventions and outcome measures were sufficiently similar, meta-analysis was performed to combine the results of the trials. The review included three trials involving a total of 146 participants. Two of these RCTs compared therapeutic ultrasound with sham ultrasound, while the third trial compared a combination of ultrasound and ultraviolet light with laser therapy and standard treatment. Neither of the two trials comparing ultrasound with sham ultrasound demonstrated a statistically significant difference in healing rates. The results of these two trials were pooled, as there was no significant heterogeneity between them, but no evidence of benefit from ultrasound therapy was found. Similarly, in the three-arm trial, there was no statistically significant difference in the proportion of ulcers healed among the treatment groups. The authors concluded that there is no evidence to support the use of therapeutic ultrasound for the treatment of pressure ulcers. However, due to the small number of trials, methodological limitations, and the small sample sizes of the included studies, the possibility of either beneficial or harmful effects cannot be definitively ruled out. Further research is necessary to clarify the role of ultrasound therapy in this context.
